turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll just do your observations before the doctor sees you. Sleeve up for me, please.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, course. Sorry we're a bit late, the car park was a nightmare, some van stuck across the disabled bays. I said to her, this is ridiculous.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You did, twice. Sleeve up, come on.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Lovely. Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 84, temperature 36.7, and your oxygen is 98 percent. Doctor won't be long.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Come on through. Looks like it's the toe that's brought you in.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the big toe, the right one. Absolute agony. Came on last night, woke me, throbbing, and it's swollen up like a sausage. Couldn't get the slipper on this morning.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It started before that. He was complaining yesterday morning in the kitchen, and I told him to ring you then.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not complaining yesterday morning. I was fine, did the bins and everything. It was last night, I'm telling you.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you say last night, and your wife thinks yesterday morning. We'll park the exact start. Definitely the right big toe?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Right one, yes. It's hot and red, and if the sheet even brushes it I could hit the ceiling.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any injury? Stubbed it, dropped something on it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I haven't knocked it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Hang on. I did kick the chair, going to the loo. That wooden one in the hall, my aunt's old chair. Caught the toe right on the leg of it. I'd completely forgotten.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I heard the yell. That was last night, about eleven.

[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): So there was a knock. I'm thinking aloud. A red hot swollen big toe coming on quickly makes me wonder about gout, particularly if it's happened before, but a direct kick can stir a toe up as well, so trauma stays on the list. Any fever or shivers?
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been properly unwell. He was sick in the night, threw up twice.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I have not been sick. I never threw up. And I wasn't feverish either, before anyone says it. I was just in pain. I even got a bit of sleep.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): All right, I'll note that you two disagree about the vomiting. Any chest pain, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, chest is fine, breathing's fine. It's just the toe. I'm tired, mind, but who wouldn't be. We were up early for the car park, which didn't help.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you had this exact thing before?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Same thing a year back. Right big toe again. I can't remember the month, spring maybe, or was it after the summer holiday. It's gone fuzzy.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It went on for a fortnight that time. He was off his feet two weeks.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): It was not a fortnight. Four or five days and I was back out in the garden. She's remembering it worse than it was.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): A previous episode about a year ago, then, and you don't agree how long it lasted. Did anyone call it gout?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The GP said it was probably gout and put me on allopurinol, to stop it coming back. Hundred milligrams, one a day.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Are you still on the allopurinol?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I stopped it in March. I felt fine, another tablet seemed pointless. Haven't touched it since.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): So allopurinol is stopped, not something you're taking now. The note mentions a water tablet.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the bendro-something, water tablet. Two and a half milligrams every morning, for my blood pressure. Been on it since last summer. Little white one.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Bendroflumethiazide. I do his box every Sunday. He does take that one, I watch him swallow it.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. And in the past, any ibuprofen, naproxen, or colchicine?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): They offered me ibuprofen last time and I never took it. Don't like the idea. I've never had colchicine. Nobody's ever given me it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): We won't put ibuprofen down as a medicine, then. Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. No allergies.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's right, he's not allergic to anything.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about beer? I have to ask, with a toe like this.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh, just a couple of pints at the weekend. He's not a big drinker.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, Saturday was the rugby, the England game, so it was more like six pints. I don't drink in the week at all. Sunday I left it. Weekends, yes, but Saturday was a proper session.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Six, then, if you say so. I was in the kitchen.

[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. None in the week, beer at the weekends, and a heavier lot on Saturday. Beer is a classic gout trigger, and bendroflumethiazide pushes the uric acid up too. Putting that with a very painful swollen big toe and a similar episode last year, my working impression is acute gout. I can't completely rule out a bruise from that kick, or an early skin infection, but gout is what I'd treat for today.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Gout. My dad had that, used to hobble round the allotment swearing at the cabbages. Sorry, tangent. So what do you do for it?

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Noted about your dad. I'm choosing between colchicine and a NSAID such as naproxen, and naproxen worries me a bit with the water tablet because of your kidneys. We'll start colchicine, five hundred micrograms twice a day by mouth, for five days. If you get bad diarrhoea on it, stop, and we'll switch you to naproxen instead.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice a day for five days. Do I take it with food, or does that spoil it?

[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): With food is better. Don't restart the allopurinol yourself while this attack is on, we'll look at that once the bloods are back. Ease off the beer, the weekend binges especially, until it settles. And rest that foot up on a cushion.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): The dog will be furious. He's a springer spaniel, mad as a box of frogs, and he knows when it's walk time.

[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): The dog can wait a few days. I also want a blood test for uric acid. Worth explaining, it can come back normal even in a real attack, so a normal number won't throw the diagnosis out. I'll add kidney function at the same time, because of the diuretic.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I can take the bloods once you're done, if the form comes through.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Please. Serum uric acid and U and Es, straight after we've finished, not this second.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Needles, lovely. I had a funny turn at the dentist once, and it wasn't even the needle, the chair tipped back too far. Anyway, ignore me.

[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll look after you. Come back and see me in a week, so we can check the toe and the uric acid. If the redness starts tracking up the foot, or you feel properly ill, don't wait the week, come back sooner or ring us.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him here. He'll say he's fine when he isn't.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't pretend. Hurts too much. Out of ten it's a nine, easy.

[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me look before you go. The right big toe is swollen and red over the joint, hot to the touch, and markedly tender. Skin is intact, with no break and no pus, and the other toes are fine. The calf is soft and not hot.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the worst bit of the whole visit, that pressing. Are we done?
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): We're done with the poking. Start the colchicine today, nurse will do the bloods, and I'll see you in a week.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): And if that uric acid comes back normal, you're still saying it can be gout? Just so I've got it straight.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's right. We treat this episode on the story and the examination, not on a single number.

spec.situation: Man with a very painful swollen big toe since last night; drinks beer at weekends, takes a water tablet; had the same 'a year back'; says no injury then recalls kicking a chair; colchicine or NSAID plan; blood uric acid test.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Pain severity, site, and current status supported; duration and 'aggravating_factors=kicking a chair' are not clearly stated as symptom details.
bad.text: Severe pain in the right big toe (category=musculoskeletal, status=present, severity=severe, duration=approximately 1 to 2 days, temporality=current, body_site=right big toe, aggravating_factors=kicking a chair, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Patient reports prior episode was 'probably gout'; no existing gout diagnosis for about 1 year stated.

omissions.text: Right big toe pain was described as throbbing, woke him from sleep, severe enough that he could not get his slipper on, and even the bedsheet brushing it caused extreme pain.

The patient initially denied any injury, then corrected himself to say he had kicked a wooden chair with the toe last night at about 11 pm; this direct trauma was specifically discussed as relevant to the differential.
Negative finding: patient denied having knocked/injured the toe initially before later recalling the chair injury.
Negative finding: patient denied shivers when asked about fever or shivers.
Pain severity was quantified by the patient as 9/10.
Examination finding omitted: the calf was soft.
The doctor explained that serum uric acid can be normal during a true acute gout attack and that diagnosis/treatment would rely on the history and examination rather than a single uric acid result.
The nurse planned to take the blood tests straight after the consultation if the form came through.
The follow-up in one week was specifically to check both the toe and the uric acid result.

Family history is recorded wrongly: the transcript only states that the patient's father had gout; it does not establish that the patient has an existing diagnosis of gout. The doctor said a prior GP had said it was 'probably gout' and the current impression was acute gout.
